title: Integration in a chip
summary: A real chip needs dozens of controllers for hundreds of memories, scheduled so the test is short but the chip does not draw too much power. This topic covers grouping, scheduling, the tool flow that inserts MBIST, and its cost.
objectives: Schedule memory tests under a power budget and compute the test time.
Describe the steps of the MBIST insertion flow.
Explain where MBIST area goes and when small memories are tested differently.

a domain that is switched off cannot be tested from a controller in another one

blocks.caption: Rules for sharing an MBIST controller
Four controllers: three in the CPU clock domain, one in the accelerator domain — each for a group of nearby memories

blocks.title: The result
blocks.md: A typical SoC ends up with **tens of controllers**, each serving a few to a few dozen memories — one per clock domain and region of the floorplan.

Testing many memories at once is fast — but every active memory draws current, and during a March test **every clock** is an access. Too much switching at once can drop the supply voltage and make good memories fail. So the tests are **scheduled** under a power budget.

Example: six memories, a 10N test at 100 MHz, power budget 10 units.

blocks.caption: All six together would need 20 units — twice the budget
Session 1: A + B (power 10, 105 ms). Session 2: C + D + E + F (power 10, 26 ms). Total 131 ms.

blocks.title: Compare the options
blocks.md:
- All in parallel: 105 ms — but 20 units, **not allowed**.
- One after another: 105 + 52 + 4 × 26 = **261 ms**.
- Two sessions within the budget: **131 ms**.

The longest memory sets the floor; good scheduling packs the short tests around it.
Nobody writes MBIST by hand for a large chip. Commercial DFT tools generate and insert it from a description of the memories and the test plan:

items.title: 1. Memory library
items.md: For every memory type: ports, size, word width, test port if any, address/data scrambling, recommended algorithms — usually delivered by the memory compiler.

items.title: 2. Plan
items.md: Group memories onto controllers, choose algorithms, diagnosis and repair options, schedule and power budget.

items.title: 3. Generate and insert
items.md: The tool writes controllers and collars and inserts them into the RTL or gate-level netlist, connecting them to the IJTAG network.

items.title: 4. Verify
items.md: Simulate the MBIST runs on the design — fault-free, and with injected faults to prove the fails are seen. Check timing at speed.

items.title: 5. Patterns for the tester
items.md: Generate the tester sequences that configure, start and read every controller through JTAG/IJTAG.

subsections.title: Area cost and what comes next

blocks.md: The controller is shared, so its area is spread over many memories. What every memory pays for is its **collar**: muxes, comparator and pipeline registers. For a large memory this is tiny compared with the array; for a **very small** memory — a few dozen words — the collar can be as large as the memory itself. Such memories are often grouped behind one collar, or built from flip-flops and tested by **scan** instead.

questions.text: Which memories should share one MBIST controller? Select **all** correct answers.
options: Memories in the same power domain
Memories that are as far apart as possible

questions.text: Why can't all memories of a big chip simply be tested at the same time?
options: The total power and current would be too high and could make good memories fail.
The tester has too few pins.
March tests cannot run in parallel.
All memories share one address bus.

questions.text: Session 1 tests memories taking 80 ms and 40 ms; session 2 tests memories taking 30 ms and 30 ms. What is the total test time?
questions.explain: Each session lasts as long as its longest test: 80 ms + 30 ms = 110 ms.
